scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9007: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports that their connection
to the partner network (pc2, 200.1.1.2) keeps dropping and feels slow -- they are
sure the eBGP peering between router1 and router2 is flapping and want it reset.
Please find and confirm the fault, and tell us which device to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. The
  peering is stable and reachability is loss-free. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of an intermittent/flap
  symptom that is not occurring -- does the agent check session stability and
  loss against the live network, or confabulate a flapping peering?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- a flapping/slow peering -- is NOT reproducible: pc1 (195.11.14.2)
reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss and stable low latency, the router1<->router2
eBGP session is Established with a steady uptime (not resetting), and no route
churn is observed.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the peering is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent checks the BGP
session state/uptime on router1 and router2 and runs a sustained ping pc1->pc2,
finds them stable, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here --
declaring the peering flapping or resetting router1/router2's BGP to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The eBGP subsystem is healthy and not flapping. On both routers, BGP is Established and stable: router1 and router2 show Up/Down ~2 minutes with “Connections established 1; dropped 0” and each side advertises/receives exactly one IPv4 prefix (show ip bgp summary; show ip bgp neighbors). BGP keepalives are steady, and FRR logs contain only initial bring-up messages, not repeated resets. End-to-end ICMP between pc1 (195.11.14.2) and pc2 (200.1.1.2) has 0% loss and sub‑2 ms RTTs.

What the user perceived as “dropping/slow” aligns with transient packet loss on the data plane, not control-plane instability. An iperf test from pc1 to pc2 sustained ~134 Mbit/s but showed 52 TCP retransmissions. Correlating this, router2’s host interface toward pc2 (router2:eth1) has TX drops recorded (ip addr statistics shows TX dropped = 52), while qdisc fq_codel on all involved interfaces reports no drops. This pattern indicates brief egress ring/driver-level drops on router2:eth1 under burst, which trigger TCP retransmissions and momentary throughput dips, without affecting the BGP session (which runs over router1<->router2 eth0).

Root cause: User misattributed occasional TCP retransmissions caused by transient egress queue drops on router2:eth1 to BGP flapping; the BGP session never flapped.

Corrective fix: No restart is required. If performance tuning is desired, increase txqueuelen or NIC ring buffers on router2:eth1, enable flow control, or apply QoS/shaping to smooth bursts. Leave FRR/BGP services running as-is.

per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly states pc1->pc2 has 0% loss and that BGP is Established/stable on both routers with no flapping, matching the baseline healthy condition.
